content: The study by Coulibaly et al. (2018) evaluated the effectiveness of the Olyset Duo bed net, which combines pyriproxyfen and permethrin, compared to a permethrin-only net in reducing clinical malaria in a rural area of Burkina Faso with highly pyrethroid-resistant vectors. This was conducted as a cluster-randomized controlled trial and published in The Lancet. The World Health Organization (WHO) has emphasized the importance of achieving and maintaining universal coverage with long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) for malaria control, as outlined in their 2017 guidelines. Additionally, WHO has provided recommendations for the proper management of old LLINs (2014) and operational manuals for indoor residual spraying (IRS) for malaria control and elimination (2015). The Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs), under the United Nations Environment Programme (2018), addresses the environmental impact of chemicals used in vector control. WHO has also convened evidence review groups to assess the comparative effectiveness of new vector control tools (2017) and provided guidelines for scaling up IRS globally (2006). Several studies have explored the impact of IRS on malaria control. For example, Abuaku et al. (2018) investigated the effect of IRS on malaria parasitemia in northern Ghana, while Tseng et al. (2008) demonstrated rapid malaria control using alpha-cypermethrin IRS in São Tomé and Príncipe. Keating et al. (2021) retrospectively evaluated the effectiveness of IRS with pirimiphos-methyl (Actellic) in Zambia. Namuganga et al. (2021) examined the consequences of stopping and restarting IRS in Uganda, and Gimnig et al. (2016) assessed the impact of IRS on malaria prevalence, clinical malaria, and anemia in western Kenya. Comparative studies, such as those by Curtis et al. (1998) and Misra et al. (1999), have evaluated the use of pyrethroids for house spraying versus bed net treatment. Abong'o et al. (2020) studied the entomological and clinical impacts of IRS with pirimiphos-methyl in Kenya, while Hailu et al. (2018) analyzed the cost-effectiveness of combining LLINs and IRS in Ethiopia. WHO has also provided guidance on combining IRS and LLINs (2014) and highlighted the risks of scaling back vector control after malaria transmission reduction (2015). Research on housing improvements, such as house screening, has shown potential for reducing malaria risk, as demonstrated by studies in Ethiopia (Getawen et al., 2018) and The Gambia (Kirby et al., 2009). WHO published an operational manual on this topic in 2013, and systematic reviews have evaluated its effectiveness (Choi et al., 2019; Walshe et al., 2017). Intermittent preventive treatment (IPT) has been studied extensively for malaria prevention in infants, pregnant women, and school-aged children. For instance, studies have assessed the cost-effectiveness of IPT in pregnancy (Sicuri et al., 2010) and the protective efficacy of IPT in infants (Kobbe et al., 2007). Clarke et al. (2008) and Nankabirwa et al. (2010) evaluated the impact of IPT on health and education outcomes in schoolchildren. Seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) has been implemented in various regions, with studies demonstrating its effectiveness at scale in West and Central Africa (2020). WHO has provided field guides for SMC implementation, emphasizing the use of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine in children. Malaria vaccines, such as RTS,S/AS01, have shown promise in clinical trials. Chandramohan et al. (2021) investigated the combination of seasonal malaria vaccination with SMC, while Datoo et al. (2021) evaluated the efficacy of the R21 vaccine in Burkina Faso. These advancements represent significant progress in malaria prevention and control.
